Refs #1672

Phases 2–5 of the four-moment design (`docs/declarative-checks/DESIGN.md`, landed with Phase 1 in #1676), plus the owner's schema ruling, one commit each.

## The schema rung

Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there. The promotion ladder gains the rung above checks: a document's shape — a required field, a closed value set, a type, a closed key set — lives in the JSON Schema the document points at with `$schema`, and a declared assertion or a coded twin restating it is a schema check in disguise. The engine now enforces it: `engine/checks/helpers/json-schema.mjs` validates the draft-2020 subset the corpus's schemas use, and the basics `schema-conformance` rule judges every JSON document whose `$schema` is a repo-relative path (every task.json in the tree validates; a rehearsal fixture carries a member's own schema-pointed document across). The phrasing is in `extracting-lessons.md`, the `prose-to-checks` skill, basics' ladder line, the checks README, the design and the inventory.

## Phase 2 — work scope (#1699)

`forbidAddedLinesMatching`, `forbidRemovedLinesMatching` (with `unlessMatchRemainsInFile` so a reworded line is not a loss), `requireCoChange`, `flagUntrackedFilesMatching`, and the rule-level `whenReplyClassIncludes` gate on the session's comment classes. Three rules land on them: `check-ships-with-test` (growth, blocking with grace), `untracked-test-file` (basics, advisory — it fired on this branch's own fixtures before they were staged), `rules-append-only` (home, advisory).

## Phase 3 — action scope (#1700)

`scope: "action"` + `guardToolCalls`: a tool, the input field it reads, and the condition. The PreToolUse hook judges the call about to run — blocking denies with the finding's text, advisory injects it as context — and `check_the_work` judges every recorded call at Stop, the backstop and the metric. The hook now watches every tool. Seven guards in basics, seven in the home pack. The shell guards anchor to a command position: the hook's first live firing, in the session that wrote it, was on the phrase inside a commit message. A call the hook denied is recorded advisory at Stop — the firing counted, no block left for the session to clear.

## Phase 4 — trigger scope (#1701)

Skill metadata `force-load-on-tool-calls` (`Bash.command /…/`, a name, or a regex over names), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`, `force-load-on-tool-results-matching`. The PreToolUse guard holds a named call until the skill is loaded; new UserPromptSubmit and PostToolUse hooks inject the load instruction; `skill-loaded-before-editing` catches at Stop what a hook never saw; every member registers the two hooks through the converge. Three operation skills carry rules that had a trigger all along — `committing`, `fetching-from-the-web` (basics), `running-the-suite` (home) — and their bullets leave `RULES.md` by the deletion test (the `rules-append-only` advisories on this branch are those deliberate removals). `writing-handover-issues`, `do-later`, `writing-migration-plans` and `merge-to-main` gain the triggers their descriptions named.

## Phase 5 — the creation path (#1702)

The ladder names the declared rung's three moments and the skill rung's triggers; `prose-to-checks` triages a candidate by where its signature lives (the inventory's classes) before the check-the-world question; the home pack names `docs/declarative-checks/rule-inventory.md` as the sweep's worklist here.

## The hooks are guests (added after review)

The harness reads exit 2 as the one block; any other exit code, a timeout, or stdout that is not JSON is an error printed beside every call it happens on, and `permissionDecision: "allow"` skips the permission prompt. So:

- **One runner.** The three per-call entries are three-line calls into `engine/hooks/hook-runner.mjs`; the judges (`*-judge.mjs`) return verdicts and never touch the process. The runner alone exits — 0, or 2 for a block on an event that can block — and turns a bad payload, an engine that fails to load, a registry that throws or whose import never settles (a 5 s deadline), or a closed stdout into exit 0 and a hook-log line. `engine-tests/hooks/hook-runner.test.mjs` drives every one of those through the real entries; the home pack's `hook-judges-never-exit` check holds the shape.
- **No auto-approval.** The advisory context carries `additionalContext` only; verified live that the harness delivers it without a `permissionDecision`.
- **Cost.** Measured with `dev/tools/hook-latency.mjs` (committed). Before: ~185 ms (PreToolUse) + ~172 ms (PostToolUse) on every call, ~250 ms each with a 5 MB transcript, because each call reloaded the registry and parsed the whole transcript. After: ~88 ms + ~80 ms regardless of transcript size — the active packs' triggers and action rules are cached under the OS temp dir behind a stat fingerprint (settings, pack dirs, manifests, declarations, skills, the deriving engine modules; `engine-tests/hooks/hook-context.test.mjs` proves each edit misses), and the transcript is parsed only once a trigger names the call. The floor is node's start plus the engine imports.
- **The review in a week.** The retrospective brief in the design gained **Hook cost** and **Hook health** rows with the recorded numbers and the durable signal (`hook_non_blocking_error` attachments in the captured transcripts); #1703 is pointed at them.

## Observed in production, in the authoring session

The canon's own hooks run this tree, so each mechanism fired for real while it was being written: a blocking guard denied a Bash call, an advisory guard's context reached the model, the PostToolUse trigger injected a skill's load instruction on a result, and the tool-call trigger held a `node --test` (and later a `git commit`) until the skill was loaded. Those are the plan's verification links V1–V3, read live rather than filed. The runner's fail-open path also ran live: in the minutes between the entries and the judges existing, the hook log shows `done exit=0 hook-failed Cannot find module` and no error reached the call.

## Verified

Full suite green (3297 tests) after rebasing onto `main`; `check_the_world` at 0 blocking; `check_the_work` clean apart from the advisories above; the rehearsal fixtures green in both modes.

content.text:
Comment class: feature

**The gap, briefly.** The transcript reader that both hooks and the Stop rule share counts a skill as loaded in two ways: a `Skill` tool call, or a `Read` of its `SKILL.md`. When you type a slash command (`/merge-to-main`, `/do-later …`), the harness expands the skill itself and records neither. So after `/merge-to-main` the tool-call trigger would still hold the first `merge_pull_request` call, and the Stop rule would flag the session as never having loaded the skill. Closes #1699

Refs #1672

Phases 2–5 of the four-moment design (`docs/declarative-checks/DESIGN.md`, landed with Phase 1 in #1676), plus the owner's schema ruling, one commit each.

## The schema rung

Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there. The promotion ladder gains the rung above checks: a document's shape — a required field, a closed value set, a type, a closed key set — lives in the JSON Schema the document points at with `$schema`, and a declared assertion or a coded twin restating it is a schema check in disguise. The engine now enforces it: `engine/checks/helpers/json-schema.mjs` validates the draft-2020 subset the corpus's schemas use, and the basics `schema-conformance` rule judges every JSON document whose `$schema` is a repo-relative path (every task.json in the tree validates; a rehearsal fixture carries a member's own schema-pointed document across). The phrasing is in `extracting-lessons.md`, the `prose-to-checks` skill, basics' ladder line, the checks README, the design and the inventory.

## Phase 2 — work scope (#1699)

`forbidAddedLinesMatching`, `forbidRemovedLinesMatching` (with `unlessMatchRemainsInFile` so a reworded line is not a loss), `requireCoChange`, `flagUntrackedFilesMatching`, and the rule-level `whenReplyClassIncludes` gate on the session's comment classes. Three rules land on them: `check-ships-with-test` (growth, blocking with grace), `untracked-test-file` (basics, advisory — it fired on this branch's own fixtures before they were staged), `rules-append-only` (home, advisory).

## Phase 3 — action scope (#1700)

`scope: "action"` + `guardToolCalls`: a tool, the input field it reads, and the condition. The PreToolUse hook judges the call about to run — blocking denies with the finding's text, advisory injects it as context — and `check_the_work` judges every recorded call at Stop, the backstop and the metric. The hook now watches every tool. Seven guards in basics, seven in the home pack. The shell guards anchor to a command position: the hook's first live firing, in the session that wrote it, was on the phrase inside a commit message. A call the hook denied is recorded advisory at Stop — the firing counted, no block left for the session to clear.

## Phase 4 — trigger scope (#1701)

Skill metadata `force-load-on-tool-calls` (`Bash.command /…/`, a name, or a regex over names), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`, `force-load-on-tool-results-matching`. The PreToolUse guard holds a named call until the skill is loaded; new UserPromptSubmit and PostToolUse hooks inject the load instruction; `skill-loaded-before-editing` catches at Stop what a hook never saw; every member registers the two hooks through the converge. A skill counts as loaded by a `Skill` call, a `Read` of its SKILL.md, or a slash command the owner typed (the harness's `<command-name>` block — the same grammar the usage fold reads, pinned by a drift guard). Three operation skills carry rules that had a trigger all along — `committing`, `fetching-from-the-web` (basics), `running-the-suite` (home) — and their bullets leave `RULES.md` by the deletion test (the `rules-append-only` advisories on this branch are those deliberate removals). `writing-handover-issues`, `do-later`, `writing-migration-plans` and `merge-to-main` gain the triggers their descriptions named.

## Phase 5 — the creation path (#1702)

The ladder names the declared rung's three moments and the skill rung's triggers; `prose-to-checks` triages a candidate by where its signature lives (the inventory's classes) before the check-the-world question; the home pack names `docs/declarative-checks/rule-inventory.md` as the sweep's worklist here.

## The hooks are guests (added after review)

The harness reads exit 2 as the one block; any other exit code, a timeout, or stdout that is not JSON is an error printed beside every call it happens on, and `permissionDecision: "allow"` skips the permission prompt. So:

- **One runner.** The three per-call entries are three-line calls into `engine/hooks/hook-runner.mjs`; the judges (`*-judge.mjs`) return verdicts and never touch the process. The runner alone exits — 0, or 2 for a block on an event that can block — and turns a bad payload, an engine that fails to load, a registry that throws or whose import never settles (a 5 s deadline), or a closed stdout into exit 0 and a hook-log line. `engine-tests/hooks/hook-runner.test.mjs` drives every one of those through the real entries; the home pack's `hook-judges-never-exit` check holds the shape.
- **No auto-approval.** The advisory context carries `additionalContext` only; verified live that the harness delivers it without a `permissionDecision`.
- **Cost.** Measured with `dev/tools/hook-latency.mjs` (committed). Before: ~185 ms (PreToolUse) + ~172 ms (PostToolUse) on every call, ~250 ms each with a 5 MB transcript, because each call reloaded the registry and parsed the whole transcript. After: ~88 ms + ~80 ms regardless of transcript size — the active packs' triggers and action rules are cached under the OS temp dir behind a stat fingerprint (settings, pack dirs, manifests, declarations, skills, the deriving engine modules; `engine-tests/hooks/hook-context.test.mjs` proves each edit misses), and the transcript is parsed only once a trigger names the call. The floor is node's start plus the engine imports.
- **The review in a week.** The retrospective brief in the design gained **Hook cost** and **Hook health** rows with the recorded numbers and the durable signal (`hook_non_blocking_error` attachments in the captured transcripts); #1703 is pointed at them.

## Observed in production, in the authoring session

The canon's own hooks run this tree, so each mechanism fired for real while it was being written: a blocking guard denied a Bash call, an advisory guard's context reached the model, the PostToolUse trigger injected a skill's load instruction on a result, and the tool-call trigger held a `node --test` (and later a `git commit`) until the skill was loaded. Those are the plan's verification links V1–V3, read live rather than filed. The runner's fail-open path also ran live: in the minutes between the entries and the judges existing, the hook log shows `done exit=0 hook-failed Cannot find module` and no error reached the call.

## Verified

Full suite green (3300 tests) after rebasing onto `main`; `check_the_world` at 0 blocking; `check_the_work` clean apart from the advisories above; the rehearsal fixtures green in both modes.

content.text:
Fixed and pushed as `b03cad39` on [PR #1711](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/pull/1711).

**The gap.** The shared transcript reader in [session-transcript.mjs](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/blob/claude/rules-declarative-checks-gol62q/engine/checks/helpers/session-transcript.mjs) decided "this skill is loaded" from two shapes only: a `Skill` tool call, or a `Read` of the skill's `SKILL.md`. A slash command you type (`/merge-to-main`, `/do-later …`) is expanded by the harness itself and leaves neither. The harness records it as a `<command-name>` block in the user turn. So after `/merge-to-main` the tool-call trigger would still have held the first `merge_pull_request` call, and the Stop rule would have reported the skill as never loaded.

**The fix.** The reader now reads that block as a third load shape. The grammar is the one the usage fold already uses for its `userCommands` count, which was written against real captured logs: leading slash dropped, a plugin prefix kept, so a plugin's `/plugin:x` never passes for a pack skill named `x`. A pack cannot import a fresh engine export, so the grammar is spelled in both places and a drift guard in the reader's test runs both parsers over one vector set in both directions. A tool result that merely contains the literal tag does not count.

**Proved.** A new hook test holds a triggered call with no load and lets it through with a transcript carrying only the typed command. Full suite green at 3300, work sweep 0 blocking.

```
engine/checks/helpers     transcript reader recognises the harness's <command-name> block as a load
```

content.content:
Pack versions are cut on main by automation, never in the pull request (#1726)
* Pack versions are cut on main by automation, never in the pull request

A change under packs/<id>/ no longer bumps that pack's version itself. The
canon-curation pack gains pack-version-bump: a worker that walks the base
branch to each pack's last bump, cuts today's next version for every pack
with a shipping change since, and commits the manifests straight onto main
with git plumbing. The canon's pack-versions.yml workflow runs it on every
push to main; the task runs it daily for the merges a GITHUB_TOKEN push never
turns into a run.

pack-version-bumped and pack-version-claimed-once are removed with every
instruction to bump by hand or write a VERSIONS.md row. VERSIONS.md becomes
a derived record: the weekly pack-version-history task retraces from git
which pull requests each version shipped and appends the missing rows on a
self-landing pull request whose policy covers only those files.

Closes #1723
Closes #1689

-- **Running the test suite** — `node --test $(git ls-files '*.test.mjs')`. There is no test
-  script, and every hand-written glob under-runs it silently: `node --test <dir>` doesn't recurse,
-  and bash `**` without `globstar` reached 37 of 65 files. `ci.yml`'s array is not authoritative.
-
-- **Wanting a different slice of a suite run's output** — redirect one run to a file and grep that
-  file. Never re-run the ~55s suite to re-slice unchanged output. (59)
-
-- **Certifying a run green that covers a new test file** — `git add` it first. `git ls-files`
-  silently excludes an unstaged file, so the run may never have executed it. (60)
-
-- **Iterating on a sweep across many files** — run only the test files the edit touches, plus
-  `check_the_work`. Spend the whole suite and `check_the_world` once, at the end: both are
-  whole-tree aggregates whose verdict cannot turn on one file, and per-edit reruns took 25 of one
-  session's 26 minutes of tool wall-clock. (61)

-  through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose).
-  Promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the
-  interactive session's.

-  matter, `curl` into the scratchpad and read from disk. On a `403` don't retry and don't try a
-  sibling URL — attribute the search snippet to the publisher instead of asserting it, and mark it
-  for re-verification.
-
-- **Hitting a sandbox or proxy that denies a fetch** — treat it as a **policy boundary, not an
-  obstacle to route around**: don't reach for an open-network runner, an ad-hoc CI workflow or a
-  push-triggered "probe", to make the request from somewhere the policy doesn't apply. Answer from
-  committed reference material or ask the owner, and say plainly that anything unverifiable is
-  unverified. Recognize a fetch tool's own signal for a domain-wide **egress block** (e.g. an
-  explicit `EGRESS_BLOCKED` error) rather than reading it as an ordinary publisher `403` — a block
-  is domain-wide, so working down a list of alternate sources for the same fact spends the same
-  denial again on each one, where a `403` is at least per-site. And never file the gap as
-  "re-verify next pass": no later agent pass can close a policy-level block either, so mark it as
-  needing a human or an unblocked environment instead.
-
-- **Committing** — one concern per commit: if two changes could each stand alone, split them, and
-  a message that wants numbered items is the split talking. Once a commit has landed, revise with a
-  new commit, never a rewrite of that one.

Refs #1672

Phases 2–5 of the four-moment design (`docs/declarative-checks/DESIGN.md`, landed with Phase 1 in #1676), plus the owner's schema ruling, one commit each.

## The schema rung

Anything a schema can enforce is better handled there. The promotion ladder gains the rung above checks: a document's shape — a required field, a closed value set, a type, a closed key set — lives in the JSON Schema the document points at with `$schema`, and a declared assertion or a coded twin restating it is a schema check in disguise. The engine now enforces it: `engine/checks/helpers/json-schema.mjs` validates the draft-2020 subset the corpus's schemas use, and the basics `schema-conformance` rule judges every JSON document whose `$schema` is a repo-relative path (every task.json in the tree validates; a rehearsal fixture carries a member's own schema-pointed document across). The phrasing is in `extracting-lessons.md`, the `prose-to-checks` skill, basics' ladder line, the checks README, the design and the inventory.

## Phase 2 — work scope (#1699)

`forbidAddedLinesMatching`, `forbidRemovedLinesMatching` (with `unlessMatchRemainsInFile` so a reworded line is not a loss), `requireCoChange`, `flagUntrackedFilesMatching`, and the rule-level `whenReplyClassIncludes` gate on the session's comment classes. Three rules land on them: `check-ships-with-test` (growth, blocking with grace), `untracked-test-file` (basics, advisory — it fired on this branch's own fixtures before they were staged), `rules-append-only` (home, advisory).

## Phase 3 — action scope (#1700)

`scope: "action"` + `guardToolCalls`: a tool, the input field it reads, and the condition. The PreToolUse hook judges the call about to run — blocking denies with the finding's text, advisory injects it as context — and `check_the_work` judges every recorded call at Stop, the backstop and the metric. The hook now watches every tool. Seven guards in basics, seven in the home pack. The shell guards anchor to a command position: the hook's first live firing, in the session that wrote it, was on the phrase inside a commit message. A call the hook denied is recorded advisory at Stop — the firing counted, no block left for the session to clear.

## Phase 4 — trigger scope (#1701)

Skill metadata `force-load-on-tool-calls` (`Bash.command /…/`, a name, or a regex over names), `force-load-on-prompts-matching`, `force-load-on-tool-results-matching`. The PreToolUse guard holds a named call until the skill is loaded; new UserPromptSubmit and PostToolUse hooks inject the load instruction; `skill-loaded-before-editing` catches at Stop what a hook never saw; every member registers the two hooks through the converge. A skill counts as loaded by a `Skill` call, a `Read` of its SKILL.md, or a slash command the owner typed (the harness's `<command-name>` block — the same grammar the usage fold reads, pinned by a drift guard). Three operation skills carry rules that had a trigger all along — `committing`, `fetching-from-the-web` (basics), `running-the-suite` (home) — and their bullets leave `RULES.md` by the deletion test (the `rules-append-only` advisories on this branch are those deliberate removals). `writing-handover-issues`, `do-later`, `writing-migration-plans` and `merge-to-main` gain the triggers their descriptions named.

## Phase 5 — the creation path (#1702)

The ladder names the declared rung's three moments and the skill rung's triggers; `prose-to-checks` triages a candidate by where its signature lives (the inventory's classes) before the check-the-world question; the home pack names `docs/declarative-checks/rule-inventory.md` as the sweep's worklist here.

## The hooks are guests (added after review)

The harness reads exit 2 as the one block; any other exit code, a timeout, or stdout that is not JSON is an error printed beside every call it happens on, and `permissionDecision: "allow"` skips the permission prompt. So:

- **One runner.** The three per-call entries are three-line calls into `engine/hooks/hook-runner.mjs`; the judges (`*-judge.mjs`) return verdicts and never touch the process. The runner alone exits — 0, or 2 for a block on an event that can block — and turns a bad payload, an engine that fails to load, a registry that throws or whose import never settles (a 5 s deadline), or a closed stdout into exit 0 and a hook-log line. `engine-tests/hooks/hook-runner.test.mjs` drives every one of those through the real entries; the home pack's `hook-judges-never-exit` check holds the shape.
- **No auto-approval.** The advisory context carries `additionalContext` only; verified live that the harness delivers it without a `permissionDecision`.
- **Cost.** Measured with `dev/tools/hook-latency.mjs` (committed). Before: ~185 ms (PreToolUse) + ~172 ms (PostToolUse) on every call, ~250 ms each with a 5 MB transcript, because each call reloaded the registry and parsed the whole transcript. After: ~88 ms + ~80 ms regardless of transcript size — the active packs' triggers and action rules are cached under the OS temp dir behind a stat fingerprint (settings, pack dirs, manifests, declarations, skills, the deriving engine modules; `engine-tests/hooks/hook-context.test.mjs` proves each edit misses), and the transcript is parsed only once a trigger names the call. The floor is node's start plus the engine imports.
- **The review in a week.** The retrospective brief in the design gained **Hook cost** and **Hook health** rows with the recorded numbers and the durable signal (`hook_non_blocking_error` attachments in the captured transcripts); #1703 is pointed at them.

## Observed in production, in the authoring session

The canon's own hooks run this tree, so each mechanism fired for real while it was being written: a blocking guard denied a Bash call, an advisory guard's context reached the model, the PostToolUse trigger injected a skill's load instruction on a result, and the tool-call trigger held a `node --test` (and later a `git commit`) until the skill was loaded. Those are the plan's verification links V1–V3, read live rather than filed. The runner's fail-open path also ran live: in the minutes between the entries and the judges existing, the hook log shows `done exit=0 hook-failed Cannot find module` and no error reached the call.

## Verified

Rebased onto `main` after #1726: the branch carries no pack version bump or `VERSIONS.md` row (versions are cut on `main`). Full suite green (3357 tests); `check_the_world` at 0 blocking; `check_the_work` at 0 blocking apart from the advisories above; the rehearsal fixtures green in both modes.

The conflicts were all in pack version files, because `main` changed the convention under the branch: since #1726 versions are cut on `main` by automation and a PR never bumps them. The world sweep then caught one thing of mine, a comment in the engine naming a pack path, which is fixed. Suite green at 3357, both sweeps at 0 blocking.

**The token accounting.** Same estimator as the session summary (words ÷ 0.75), per bullet, from the branch's diff of every `RULES.md` against the merge base. Phase 1 (#1676) touched no `RULES.md`.

| Movement | rules | tokens |
|---|---|---|
| Relegated to trigger-loaded skills | 7 | 548 |
| Eliminated in favour of checks | 0 | 0 |
| Added to `RULES.md` | 2 | 114 |
| Net change to always-loaded prose | | −434 |

The 548 relegated tokens: basics gave up "Committing" (57), "Needing exact text from the web" (75) and "Hitting a sandbox or proxy that denies a fetch" (203) to the `committing` and `fetching-from-the-web` skills; the home pack gave up its four suite rules (213) to `running-the-suite`. Each now loads only when its tool call or result happens.

The zero is the honest number and a gap. Every rule that became a guard or a work check kept its bullet. Twelve such bullets still stand, 724 tokens in all: four in basics (Grep context flag, wake-up prompt, pipe through tail, pkill self-match, 309 tokens) and eight in the home pack (AskUserQuestion cost, bare sleep, GitHub through the shell, list calls without fields, `commit -a`, merge of `main`, `git pull` on a shallow clone, rules append-only, 415 tokens). # Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](https://github.com/missingbulb/Claudinite/tree/main/packs) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **End every turn with a blockquote callout** — `> ✅ All done`, or `> ⚠️ Still open: …` listing what remains — never hedged in prose.
- **"LGTM"** merges the change at hand into `main` (`merge-to-main` skill); it approves that change only, never later work.
- **"bump version"** raises the project's version; the project's own workflow decides how it changes and which files change.
- **In the conversation**: link every source-controlled document you edit, display every image you edit, link every issue/PR number.
- **Ask every decision or approval through an `AskUserQuestion` popup, never prose** — one question per item, each with its case.
- **Enclose anything the owner will lift elsewhere** — a prompt, a message, copy to paste — in one delimited block, boundaries unmistakable.
- **Prefix a prompt for another session, inside its block, with a disclaimer**: Claude wrote it — examine inconsistencies, don't follow blindly.
- **Open a pull request right after committing to a branch**, unasked — overriding Claude Code's default of waiting to be told.
- **When handing over a PR to review, describe the folders the change touched in the conversation, in a text box** — a brief line per folder saying what changed there. Show non-test folders only, and ignore README files, comment-only changes, and history-keeping updates (a version bump, a changelog or `VERSIONS.md` row).
- **Keep working through a multi-step plan without pausing for approval of each step** — aggregate the steps into one substantial change to review, and stop only for an action that reaches the world (a release, a fleet-wide effect, anything irreversible) or a decision only the owner can make.
- **Never schedule a self check-in to poll a PR** — no recurring wake-up, routine, or `send_later` re-arm that re-reads a PR's state, CI or mergeability on a timer. Act on PR events when they arrive; when nothing has arrived, end the turn.

- bug-investigation: Method for investigating a bug and pinning down its root cause. Use when investigating a bug report, when a fix didn't hold or a bug recurs, or when a report doesn't reproduce against main.
- ci-performance-evaluation: Method for finding where a repo's CI time actually goes and what is worth fixing. Use when CI feels slow, when investigating a runtime regression, or when the weekly ci-performance task hands you a finding.
- committing: How a commit is cut — one concern per commit, the issue it references, a landed commit revised only by a new one, files staged by name. Use before any git commit.
- do-later: File a change to be made AFTER the work in flight — a well-defined issue, marked for the queue and blocked behind the current PR/issue and behind the previous deferral, so repeated asks chain. Use when the owner says "/do-later …", "do this after this lands", or otherwise defers a change instead of derailing the session.
- extract-from-activity: Mine a window of a repo's commits, merged PRs and issue activity for durable, reusable lessons and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from repo artifacts — the growth-extract task's activity half, or an owner asking what a recent stretch of work taught.
- extract-from-conversations: Mine an agent-user conversation — a captured conversation log or the live session — for friction-driven lessons (misunderstandings, backtracks, measured wall-time waits) and land them in the repo's own local packs. Use when extracting lessons from a session transcript or the conversation-logs branch, or when an owner asks for a retrospective.
- fetching-from-the-web: Reading a page or a file from the web in a session — exact bytes over a summarizing fetch, and what a 403 or an egress block means. Use before any WebFetch or curl, and when a fetch is denied.
- file-placement: Where a file should live — the reference-distance metric, the high-reach code smell, and the mandated-location, test-location and plugin-contract exemptions. Use before placing, moving, or renaming a file, or when reviewing where one lives.
- generate-project-instructions: Decompose a project into its pack facets (working-style class, technology, aspect, domain) and author the canon packs those facets earn. Use from a canon when a project's evidence shows a facet its shelf does not yet home — the curation stages' pack-writing method, and an owner's when asking what a project has taught the shelf.
- git-github-advanced: Git/GitHub procedures beyond the baseline lifecycle. Use for commit layering, recovering a branch after a squash-merge, CI-trigger rules, GitHub Actions gotchas, or merge-relocation traps.
- github-actions-scheduling: What a GitHub Actions `schedule:` trigger actually guarantees — late fires, dropped fires, the 60-day disable — and how to build and describe scheduled work around it. Use when adding, changing, explaining, or debugging anything that runs on a cron in GitHub Actions.
- growth-dedup: Prune a repo's local packs of items the mounted Claudinite canon now covers — remove, strip to residue, or track a wording drift, never grow an entry. Use when the growth dedup task runs, or when asked to reconcile or dedup local packs against the canon.
- improve-comments: Improve the comments in a repo's own source — delete the ones that restate the code or narrate a past edit, correct the ones that have drifted from what the code now does, and add the why where only a reader's guess carries it. Use when working a repo's comments as their own pass (the tidy-repo pack's improve-comments task), never as a side effect of another change.
- merge-to-main: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
- production-retrospective: Design and file the review that comes back on its own once a larger element has lived in production long enough to judge — is it working, misused, overused, underused — read from its real production record against expectations written down when the element was designed. Use when designing a larger element (the brief is authored then), when filing a migration plan's chain (the retrospective is its last link), when a merge completes a design-doc'd element, or when defining a new retrospective class for a pack, a repo, or the fleet.
- prose-to-checks: Mine pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, when the weekly prose-to-checks sweep runs, or as the upgrade pass over prose a growth-extract run just wrote.
- repo-text-sweeps: Mechanics for grep/sed sweeps, renames, and path relocations across a repo. Use before a bulk find-replace, a rename, or moving files — and after one, to catch silently broken references.
- running-the-suite: Running this repo's test suite — the one command that covers it, reading a run's output from a file instead of re-running it, iterating on the tests an edit touches, and staging a new test file before certifying a run. Use before any node --test.
- single-issue-triage: Triage one open issue and take the first applicable action — close-if-implemented, needs-decision, blocked, quick-win, or leave. Use when acting on a single issue; "implemented in main" must be verified against main's current content and the default is to comment, not close (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-issues task hands you issues to triage).
- single-pr-status: Assess one open pull request's landed status — keep-open, or closeable (merged, already-in-main, superseded, stale) — read-only. Use when triaging whether a single PR should stay open, judging by its commits and diff not its title (e.g. the tidy-repo pack's tidy-prs task hands you PRs to assess).
- unattended-agents: Architecture and practices for unattended, automation-invoked agents and recurring routines. Use when building, structuring, or running an AI agent, a scheduled routine, or a multi-stage agent pipeline.
- verify-in-production: Decide whether a change that has merged can only be proven in production, and if so file the verification that comes back on its own once it is live. Use immediately after the merge, beside the conversation capture — never before, and not on request.
- working-with-generated-files: Working with a file a test or tool generates — naming it, changing the generator rather than the file, and resolving its merge conflicts by regenerating. Loaded for any edit of a GENERATED file.
- writing-claudinite-skills: Authoring or changing a skill in the Claudinite corpus — SKILL.md conventions, where a skill's checks and tests live, catalog and pack wiring. Use when creating or editing a pack's skills/<name>/ in the canon; a consumer project's own agent docs are authoring-agent-docs' turf.
- writing-handover-issues: How to write a task list a PERSON will execute — a handover issue, an adoption checklist, a "steps only a human can do" list. Use when filing or editing any issue whose body asks a human to click, set, register or copy something. Not for issues describing work you will do yourself.
- writing-migration-plans: Where a plan and a design live, and how to order a plan's phases so nothing stalls mid-run — the plan is a tracking issue (never a plan document in the repo), the design doc carries only the end state with rationale and alternatives; front-load the out-of-band setup, write ALL the code including the cleanup and take one approval for the stack, then chain every execution step to the verification of the one before it as a queued continuation, size the links (how many PRs, what each one's diff is predicted to touch and the automerge policy that prediction becomes) and write the chain to survive a policy park, a red CI or a PR closed unmerged, and keep the tracking issue append-only while implementing. Use BEFORE writing any DESIGN.md, migration plan, phased implementation plan, rollout or cutover plan — including the moment you are about to create a docs/<initiative>/ file — when asked to run a plan as a chain of ad-hoc tasks, and when working through a plan's tracking issue.
- writing-pack-prose: How pack prose is written — RULES.md rules, SKILL.md bodies and check text in a Claudinite pack, local or canon — brevity, structure, triggerability, findability, and the per-pack references doc. - writing-repo-scanning-checks: How a check that scans the repo picks its file set, strips comments before matching a forbidden token, and proves itself silent against real sources. Loaded for any edit of a coded or declared check.
- writing-tasks: The contract a Claudinite task is written to — the declaration's fields, the code-work and agentic phases, the precondition as the only decision point, ordering, and how a work item converges. Use when writing or changing a tasks/<name>/task.json or its worker, or when a task-declaration check fires.
- writing-tests: Practices for writing tests you can trust. Use before writing or changing any test — see-it-fail discipline, snapshot/golden rules, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, fuzzy-metric gating.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. - dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own.
